gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a measured figure for how much energy these banks actually deliver. Techtest.org (Michael Barton) measured the UGREEN Nexode 20,000 mAh 165 W, ChatGPT's 'best overall' pick, at 62.5–66.4 Wh, and the Anker Prime 26K, labelled 99.75 Wh (just under the 100 Wh limit), at 79.6–89.8 Wh: about 15–25 Wh more usable energy than a 20,000 mAh bank while still being allowed in carry-on without airline approval.
standout_why: I read the RuntimeWise airline rules page (result 16). It names products only for bans (Anker A1647/A1681/A1689 on Air Canada, EcoFlow/Jackery/Bluetti on American) and says its own mAh-to-Wh table is 'calculated estimates', not measurements. The cited aa.com page returned HTTP 403. The cited IATA PDF came back as unreadable binary, and my request to extract its text locally was refused, so I read neither in full. Going by their sources (FAA, IATA, airline baggage pages), these are rules documents, not product tests. ChatGPT's own answer gives only nominal Wh from its 3.7 V arithmetic (20,000 mAh = 74 Wh). None of the results says that usable output runs 74–95% of the label, or how far apart the measured numbers for these candidates are.
decides: The finding backs a ~99.5 Wh pick (Anker Prime 26K or EcoFlow RAPID Pro) for anyone charging a laptop. Both delivered 75–90 Wh in testing, against 62–66 Wh for ChatGPT's UGREEN 20K pick, and both held 140 W steadily. For phone-only travel it supports a small, efficient 10K: the INIU P55L-E2 delivered 94–95% of its rating, against 74–85% for ChatGPT's Anker Nano A1638 pick, which also dropped to about 27 W after 13–16 minutes. It counts against the Nitecore NB20000 Gen3 on our page, which delivered only 62–74% of its rating.
